metadata.title: Finding an Unknown Joining Time or Investment Duration
metadata.description: Use a stated profit ratio to solve when a partner joined or how long capital remained invested.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Translate a profit ratio into equality or proportionality of capital-time products. Let an unknown entry time be x months and express the remaining duration as T−x; alternatively let the unknown duration be x and solve from known capital and profit shares. Keep x within the valid business period and check the result by substituting it back into the original ratio. Include equal-profit and unequal-profit conditions, two or three partners, and distinguish joining after x months from investing for x months. Ground in solved examples 10–11, 14 and objective patterns 47–50, 57–58.

content.text: Finding an Unknown Joining Time or Investment Duration: Use a stated profit ratio to solve when a partner joined or how long capital remained invested. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Finding an Unknown Joining Time or Investment Duration asks you to decide what determines each person’s share or assigned amount. Use a stated profit ratio to solve when a partner joined or how long capital remained invested. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. A stated profit ratio reveals a relationship between capital-time products. Write the partner or user labels and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

If A:B profit is p:q, then C_A t_A:C_B t_B=p:q. When one duration is unknown, isolate it and distinguish duration from the join delay. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once the quantities use compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: A invests ₹76,000 for 12 months. B invests ₹57,000 and receives half of A’s share. B’s duration solves 76,000×12:57,000×t=2:1, giving t=8 months. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Set the proportion before cross-multiplying so the ratio order stays visible. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. Substitute the solved duration back into both weighted contributions and reduce; verify it fits the business term. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Do not equate the money investments to the profit ratio unless durations match. Keep p paired with A and q paired with B. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. If asked when B joined a 12-month business, convert 8 months invested into joining after 4 months. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for finding an unknown joining time or investment duration without relying on a memorized answer pattern.

A invests ₹80000 for a 12-month business. B invests ₹60000 and joins later. If A:B profit shares are 2:1, how many months after the start did B join?

inlineData.prompt: A invests ₹80000 for a 12-month business. B invests ₹60000 and joins later. If A:B profit shares are 2:1, how many months after the start did B join?
hints: Distinguish B’s months invested from the delay before B joined.
First solve B's duration from C_A T : C_B t = 2:1; subtract that duration from 12.
inlineData.explanation: A's capital-time is 80000×12=960000. For ratio 2:1, B's required weight is 480000; at ₹60000 per month B's duration is 8 months. Thus B joined after 12−8=4 months. Verify by substituting both weights.
